one_liner: C++-embedded JIT DSL whose copy-and-patch backend generates code about 100x faster than LLVM -O0, with 14% faster output.
what_it_does: PochiVM lets C++ code build a program at runtime through a C-like embedded DSL (NewFunction, Declare, For, If, Return, plus calls into arbitrary C++ classes and templates) and then run that program through one of three backends: an AST interpreter, a copy-and-patch baseline compiler (called FastInterp in the code), or LLVM 10 at -O0..-O3. It is not a drop-in for LLVM: you write the program through its API rather than handing it LLVM IR. The repo also contains the 600-line TPC-H query-compiler prototype used in the OOPSLA 2021 paper.
how_it_is_fast: Copy-and-patch: at install time Clang compiles 98,831 pre-built machine-code 'stencils' (one per AST node type and configuration) with holes for constants, jump targets and stack offsets; at runtime code generation just memcpys the matching stencils and patches the holes, with no instruction selection or IR. Stencils use continuation-passing style with tail calls lowered to jumps and the GHC calling convention, so the next stencil is reached by a jump and values stay in registers (a lightweight register-allocation protocol); further gains come from jump removal, supernodes and block alignment. Generation is linear in program size, unlike LLVM's non-linear passes.
when_to_use: A C++ engine that generates many short-lived programs (query, rule or expression engines) where compile latency dominates: TPC-H Q5 generates code in 178 us versus 0.25 s with LLVM -O3, and the query itself runs in under 0.1 s.
Replacing an AST or bytecode interpreter: the paper measures copy-and-patch code 6x-27x faster than its AST interpreter for 2-3x the (still negligible) setup cost.
A two-tier design: the same DSL program can go to copy-and-patch first and to LLVM -O2/-O3 later for hot, long-running code, since all three backends take one AST.
Studying or prototyping copy-and-patch itself: the stencil generator, CPS/GHC calling-convention tricks and paper harness are all in the repo.
when_not_to_use: Long-running generated code: LLVM -O1..-O3 output is 22%-25% faster; in the paper's Q5 example the -O3 compile cost pays back only after about 21 s of execution.
Anything other than Linux on x86-64: the docs say only Linux is supported, the build runs in an Ubuntu 18.04 Docker image with the x86_64 LLVM 10.0.0 release, and stencils are x86-64 machine code.

Production dependencies: abandoned since 2021-09-09, an open build failure (issue #4, 2024: cp of libtinfo.so.5 into shared_libs gets Permission denied), no packaged release (the project template is marked UNDONE), and the docs say the test suite fails in the production build.
When you already emit LLVM IR: PochiVM only compiles programs written through its own DSL.
Tight footprint: the stencil library takes 14 min on 6 threads to build and 17.5 MB of memory at runtime.

integration.form: source-drop (fork the repository and build your project inside its Docker/CMake tree; no installable library)
integration.dependencies: Clang and LLVM 10.0.0 (pinned in dockerfile/Dockerfile), Docker, CMake with Ninja, ccache (CMakeLists aborts without it), Python 3 build script, libtinfo; gtest vendored
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 with Clang/LLVM 10.0.0 as pinned by the Docker image; other LLVM versions not documented
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 only (docs: 'Only Linux is supported at the moment')
integration.thread_safety: Build state lives in a thread_local PochiVMContext (thread_pochiVMContext), so each thread builds its own modules; sharing a module across threads is not documented

gotchas: Known unfixed miscompile risk: pochivm/cast_expr_fastinterp.cpp carries 'TODO: FIXME: casting int to float changes the register location..' (commit 591c506, July 2021); the copy-and-patch path emits reinterpret_cast between integer and floating types as a no-op even though the value must move between register classes. Avoid int/float bit casts in copy-and-patch mode; the TPC-H queries do not use them and their correctness tests check copy-and-patch output against expected results.

Harness differs from the paper's stated method: the paper reports averages of at least 100 runs, but the public BenchmarkTpchQuery and GetBestResultOfRuns report the minimum of 10 runs (20 for copy-and-patch code generation). Each LLVM timing also builds a fresh LLJIT, about 1 ms of fixed startup that the paper amortizes only in the microbenchmarks. This is a reproduction gap, not invalid evidence.

For a fair comparison the benchmark LLVM JIT is pinned to the x86-64 baseline target (SSE2, no AVX), the same as the stencils. Neither backend uses AVX, so absolute -O3 numbers are below what -march=native would give.

The DSL has no const, volatile or rvalue-reference types, and generated function prototypes may take and return only fundamental types. C++ call inlining and LLVM optimization happen only in release/production builds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: TPDE takes ordinary LLVM IR, compiles 10-20x faster than LLVM -O0 at similar code quality and is maintained, so prefer it when you have IR. PochiVM's copy-and-patch is roughly ten times faster again at code generation but requires its DSL and is abandoned; pick it to embed a C++ code generator with interpreter-like startup, or as the reference for the technique also used by WasmNow and CPython's copy-and-patch JIT.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' OOPSLA 2021 paper (Xu and Kjolstad), on 8 hand-planned TPC-H queries over a scale-factor-0.3 database on an Intel i7-7700HQ, copy-and-patch generated code up to 276x faster than LLVM 10.0.0 at -O0 and 1083x-1435x faster than -O1..-O3 (stencils built by Clang++ 10 -O3 -DNDEBUG, LLVM limited to x86-64 baseline features). Its code ran 14% faster than -O0 and 22%-25% slower than -O1..-O3 on average, and the AST interpreter was 6x-27x slower; the public harness reproduces these runs but reports the best of 10-20 runs rather than the paper's stated averages.
status_note: Abandoned research prototype (last commit 2021-09-09, open 2024 build-failure issue). The Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception grant is stated only in the README (no LICENSE file), so treat it as reference code or a fork starting point, not a maintained dependency.
